title: The famous army-size figures are chronicle rhetoric, not a census
evidence: George Sphrantzes reports 200,000 Ottoman men and 400 vessels, but modern historians cited in the sources reviewed prefer a range of roughly 60,000-80,000, and one database entry (EBSCO) is internally inconsistent between 120,000 (body text) and 160,000 (infobox) for the same campaign.
interpretation: Round, very large numbers in 15th-century chronicles served a rhetorical purpose (magnifying the scale of the threat and the achievement of surviving or conquering it) as much as a documentary one. A data-literate reading of 1453 should present the Ottoman force as 'large and numerically dominant, order of magnitude in the tens of thousands' rather than committing to any single headline number - and should flag that even reputable-looking reference sites can contradict themselves within a single article.

title: The defender count is unusually well-attested for a medieval battle - and still has two competing versions
evidence: Sphrantzes explicitly says he was ordered to keep the true defender count secret, and gives 4,773 Greeks plus about 200 foreigners in one translation; a variant wording (4,983 Greeks, just under 2,000 foreigners) circulates in later retellings tied to the disputed 'Pseudo-Sphrantzes' text.
interpretation: Unlike the Ottoman force size, the Byzantine defender count comes from a named individual who says he personally compiled it - a rare level of documentary specificity for 1453. But the existence of two different numeric traditions under the same author's name, one of them linked to a text now identified as a 16th-century forgery, is a caution against treating even 'the primary source figure' as a single settled number without checking which version and manuscript tradition is being cited.

title: The single most consequential dated event may be the 22 April overland ship transfer, not the final assault itself
evidence: Two independent source types - a scholarly reference (Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium) and a popular synthesis (World History Encyclopedia) - converge on approximately 70 Ottoman ships hauled overland into the Golden Horn on 22 April, opening a second naval front five weeks before the city fell.
interpretation: Cross-source convergence on a specific number is rare in this dataset (see the source_claims ledger for many cases where it does not happen), which raises confidence that this maneuver is reasonably well documented, and supports treating it as a hinge point: it forced an already outnumbered garrison to defend a second, previously safer, stretch of wall.

title: Population recovery after the conquest was not a single event but a decades-long, occasionally reversed process
evidence: An initial 1453 wave of resettled Anatolians had returned home by autumn according to Oz; a 1467 plague killed over 600 people; yet the city still grew enough to reach 16,324 recorded households by 1477.
interpretation: Repopulating a war-depopulated capital required sustained, repeated policy intervention (forced transfers, incentives, patriarchal reappointment) across at least a decade, and even then was vulnerable to shocks like plague. A single 'population before vs after 1453' comparison risks flattening a genuinely bumpy recovery trajectory into a clean before/after story.

title: Wall-length and wall-dimension figures disagree by margins too large to treat as rounding
evidence: Reported land-wall lengths range from 5.7 km to 6.67 km depending on whether the Blachernae extension is included; inner-wall tower counts range from 96 to effectively 192 depending on whether outer-wall towers are counted separately.
interpretation: These are not contradictions in the historical record so much as differences in what each source is measuring (which wall segment, which count basis). A rigorous data project should report such figures as ranges tied to an explicit scope, rather than picking whichever single number looks most citable.

title: The Ottoman internal debate on 25 May complicates a purely 'overwhelming force' narrative of the outcome
evidence: Four days before the city fell, the Oxford Dictionary of Byzantium records that the grand vizier Halil Pasha advised the sultan to abandon the siege.
interpretation: If the outcome had been a foregone conclusion given the forces involved, there would be little reason for the Ottoman high command to debate retreat this late. This single, well-attested episode is a useful check against deterministic narratives that treat 1453 as inevitable from the moment the siege began; it is better read as a case where multiple structural disadvantages for the defenders (SF01-SF06 in strategic_factors.csv) compounded to produce an outcome that still required late, contested decisions to bring about.

title: 'Constantinople became Istanbul in 1453' overstates the pace of the political and demographic transition
evidence: Necipoglu dates the strategic relocation of the Ottoman capital itself to 1459, not 1453; Topkapi Palace was not completed until 1478; the first solid post-conquest population register is 1477, twenty-four years after the conquest.
interpretation: Popular narratives often compress a multi-decade institutional and demographic transformation into the single date of the conquest. The dataset's own timeline (campaign_timeline.csv, rows C27-C44) shows the city functioning under direct Ottoman military control for years before its full re-establishment as a resourced, populated, monumentally rebuilt capital.

title: Modern population figures for Istanbul are themselves a moving target across even a few years of official statistics
evidence: Address-Based Population Registration System results for the province show 15,029,231 (2017), 15,840,900 (2021), approximately 15.7 million (2023), and 15,754,053 (end of 2025) - with the 2023 and 2025 figures suggesting a possible plateau or slight decline after 2021 rather than uninterrupted growth.
interpretation: Even with a modern administrative register (not a historical estimate), year-to-year province population figures for a megacity are not simply monotonically increasing; a data-driven historical project should resist assuming that 'more recent equals bigger' and should chart the actual reported values rather than an assumed growth curve.

title: This dataset's own source register is itself an analytical finding: reliable numeric claims about 1453 are the exception, not the rule
evidence: Of the 24 entries in the source_claims ledger, the great majority document a disagreement, an unverifiable attribution, or a single-source figure rather than a converged, well-corroborated number; only a handful (e.g. the ~70-ship overland transfer, CL17) show independent convergence across source tiers.
interpretation: A portfolio-quality analysis of a medieval siege should treat 'building a defensible number' as itself the hard analytical work, worth surfacing as a finding, rather than a preliminary step to be hidden behind a single clean chart.
